hook: A gardener's foster son who became the first emperor in history.

pages.x: A legend written down long after his death says Sargon was born in secret to a priestess, who set him adrift on the Euphrates in a basket of reeds sealed with tar. A man drawing water for the fields pulled him out and raised him as a gardener, and the goddess Ishtar fell in love with him. Moses would later have a very similar story.

pages.t: Cupbearer to the king of Kish
pages.x: The real Sargon first appears as cupbearer to Ur-Zababa, king of the city of Kish, a trusted job close to the king. Around 2334 BC he took the throne for himself. He called himself Sharru-kin, "the true king", perhaps because he had no royal blood to boast of.

Sargon conquered the proud cities of Sumer one by one. He beat Lugalzagesi of Uruk and led him in a neck stock to the temple gate at Nippur, then marched to the Persian Gulf and, as he boasted, washed his weapons in the sea. His armies went on to Syria and the Cedar Forest. It is often called the first empire in history.

pages.t: A capital no one has found
pages.x: He ruled from a new city, Akkad, where ships moored from as far as the Indus Valley. He boasted that 5,400 men ate bread before him every day, maybe the first standing army. His language, Akkadian, became the language of diplomacy across the Middle East for 2,000 years. Yet the ruins of Akkad itself have never been found.

pages.t: The first author we know by name
pages.x: Sargon made his daughter Enheduanna high priestess of the moon god at Ur. She wrote hymns to the goddess Inanna and signed them with her own name, which makes her the first author in history known by name, more than a thousand years before Homer.

Sargon showed that one king could rule many cities and peoples from one capital, with an army, officials and a shared language. The kings of Assyria and Babylon copied him for two thousand years, and every empire since has followed his pattern.
pts: Built what is often called the first empire
Ruled from the Persian Gulf to the Mediterranean coast
His legend inspired kings for two thousand years
